chapters.1.lds: The lesson asks readers to consider power and mercy together in God’s character. How does the broken yoke explain Judah’s welcome for the message?
chapters.1.summary: This book is a message about Nineveh, the capital of Assyria. The LORD is slow to anger and great in power. He will not leave the guilty unpunished. Mountains quake before him, and no one can stand against his anger. He is good and a refuge in the day of trouble. He will make a full end of those who plot against him. He tells Judah he will break Assyria’s yoke. A messenger on the mountains brings news of peace.
chapters.2.lds: What does the lion’s stored prey suggest about the city’s wealth?
chapters.2.summary: An attacker advances against Nineveh. Shields are red, and chariots flash like torches in the streets. The river gates are opened, and the palace collapses. The city is stripped, and its women moan like doves. People flee, and no one turns back. Plunderers carry off endless silver and gold. Nahum asks where the lions’ den is now. The lion once filled his caves with torn prey.
chapters.3.lds: Why does the final question connect the listeners’ applause with the city’s cruelty?
chapters.3.summary: Nahum cries woe to the city of blood, full of lies and plunder. Horsemen charge, and the dead lie in heaps. Nineveh sold nations by her charms and will be put to shame. No one will mourn her. She is no better than Thebes, the great city on the Nile. Thebes went into exile, and its infants were killed. Nineveh’s forts will fall like ripe figs. Her wound cannot be healed, and all who hear of it clap their hands.
